title: What is data enrichment?
explain: Enrichment means taking a bare fact (an IP address, a domain, a CVE number) and adding context until someone can make a decision with it. A raw IP tells you nothing. An IP that belongs to a bulletproof hosting company, was seen yesterday running a known ransomware C2 server, and talked to your client's firewall at 3am tells you to act.
analogy: A raw indicator is a car number plate. Enrichment is running the plate: owner, insurance, where it was last seen, whether it is reported stolen.
uk_angle: UK clients mostly want three answers: does this affect us, how bad is it, and what do we do. Every enrichment step should move you closer to one of those answers.
enrichment_tip: Use a fixed checklist per indicator type so every analyst adds the same fields: who owns it, where it is, how bad it is, when it was seen, who else reported it.
try_today: Pick one IP from today's brief. Write down five facts about it using RIPEstat (stat.ripe.net) and AbuseIPDB. That is enrichment.
quiz_q: In one sentence, what is the goal of enrichment?
quiz_a: To add enough context to a raw indicator that someone can make a decision with it.

title: The Pyramid of Pain
explain: David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain ranks indicators by how much it hurts the attacker when you block them. Bottom to top: hash values (trivial to change), IP addresses (easy), domain names (simple), network and host artefacts (annoying), tools (challenging), TTPs: tactics, techniques and procedures (tough).
analogy: Blocking a hash is like confiscating a burglar's gloves. Blocking a TTP is like making every window in the street burglar-proof.
uk_angle: Many UK SMEs only receive IP and hash blocklists. Enrichment that climbs the pyramid (which tool, which technique) gives them protection that lasts longer than a day.
enrichment_tip: For every hash or IP you share, try to add the tool name and the ATT&CK technique. That moves your intel up the pyramid.
try_today: Take one malware story from the brief and write down: one hash, one domain, one tool name, one technique. Label each with its pyramid level.
quiz_q: Which is harder for an attacker to change: an IP address or a technique (TTP)?
quiz_a: A technique. TTPs sit at the top of the pyramid because changing them means changing how the attacker works.

title: CVSS vs EPSS vs KEV
explain: CVSS (0-10) says how bad a bug could be if exploited. EPSS (0-1, from FIRST.org) estimates the chance it will be exploited in the next 30 days. KEV (CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list) says it is already being exploited. Severity, likelihood, reality.
analogy: CVSS is how deep the river is. EPSS is the chance it floods this month. KEV is: it is flooding now.
uk_angle: Cyber Essentials requires critical and high-risk updates to be applied within 14 days. Using KEV and EPSS helps clients decide which of those to do on day one rather than day fourteen.
enrichment_tip: Never send a CVE to a client with only a CVSS score. Always add EPSS percentile and KEV status, plus whether they run the product.
try_today: Look at the vulnerability table in today's brief. Find the CVE with the highest EPSS. Is it on KEV? What product is it?
quiz_q: Which of the three tells you a vulnerability is already being used in real attacks?
quiz_a: KEV. CVSS is severity and EPSS is predicted likelihood.

title: The NCSC and what it gives you for free
explain: The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is the UK's technical authority for cyber security and part of GCHQ. It publishes advisories, joint alerts with Five Eyes partners, guidance, and runs free services for UK organisations.
analogy: Think of it as the Met Office for cyber: it forecasts, warns, and publishes guidance, but you still have to bring your own umbrella.
uk_angle: Free NCSC services worth knowing: Early Warning (alerts you about malicious activity linked to your IPs and domains), Active Cyber Defence tools, Exercise in a Box, and the Suspicious Email Reporting Service.
enrichment_tip: When a story mentions a threat, check whether the NCSC has a matching advisory. An NCSC citation is a strong credibility boost for UK clients.
try_today: Visit ncsc.gov.uk and find the Early Warning service page. Note which of your clients could sign up.
quiz_q: Which UK intelligence agency is the NCSC part of?
quiz_a: GCHQ.

title: NCSC Early Warning: free enrichment for UK clients
explain: Early Warning is a free NCSC service. An organisation registers its IP addresses and domain names, and the NCSC sends alerts when those assets show up in threat feeds: infections, open vulnerable services, or links to attacker infrastructure.
analogy: It is like a neighbourhood watch that already knows your house number and phones you when someone suspicious is spotted outside.
uk_angle: For a UK MSSP or consultancy this is a cheap win: help each client register. The alerts become another enrichment source tied to their exact assets.
enrichment_tip: Keep a list of each client's public IP ranges and domains. The same list powers Early Warning, Shodan checks, and matching IOCs against clients.
try_today: Draft a one-line email to a client explaining Early Warning and why they should register.
quiz_q: What two kinds of asset does an organisation register with Early Warning?
quiz_a: IP addresses and domain names.

title: The Admiralty Code: grading sources
explain: The Admiralty (NATO) system grades intel with a letter and a number. Letter = source reliability (A completely reliable to E unreliable, F cannot be judged). Number = information credibility (1 confirmed by other sources to 5 improbable, 6 cannot be judged). B2 means usually reliable source, probably true.
analogy: Like judging a football rumour: is it from the club's official account (A) or a random fan page (E)? And do other outlets confirm it (1) or does it sound made up (5)?
uk_angle: The system has British Navy roots and UK police and government analysts still use versions of it, so UK public sector clients recognise it straight away.
enrichment_tip: Add an Admiralty grade to every item you forward. The dashboard's 'also reported by' list helps you judge the number: more independent sources means closer to 1.
try_today: Grade the top three stories in today's brief, for example B2 or C3, and write one line on why.
quiz_q: In the grade 'B2', what does the B describe and what does the 2 describe?
quiz_a: B is source reliability (usually reliable). 2 is information credibility (probably true).

title: Traffic Light Protocol (TLP 2.0)
explain: TLP labels tell the reader who they may share information with. TLP:CLEAR = anyone. TLP:GREEN = your community, not public. TLP:AMBER = your organisation and its clients who need to know. TLP:AMBER+STRICT = your organisation only. TLP:RED = named recipients only, no further sharing.
analogy: Like party invitations: CLEAR is a public poster, GREEN is the group chat, AMBER is your family, RED is a whisper to one person.
uk_angle: UK information sharing groups and NCSC partners use TLP. Labelling your client briefs correctly shows maturity and keeps you trusted.
enrichment_tip: Enrichment can change the TLP. Mixing a public IOC with a client's internal log data makes the result sensitive, so label it AMBER or stricter.
try_today: Decide a TLP label for today's brief if you forwarded it to a client. What would change if you added their log data?
quiz_q: Which TLP label means 'share with anyone, publicly'?
quiz_a: TLP:CLEAR.

title: The PHIA probability yardstick
explain: The UK Professional Head of Intelligence Assessment (PHIA) yardstick links words to probability ranges so 'likely' means the same thing to everyone. Roughly: remote chance (under 5%), highly unlikely (10-20%), unlikely (25-35%), realistic possibility (40-50%), likely (55-75%), highly likely (80-90%), almost certain (95% and above).
analogy: Like a weather forecast saying '70% chance of rain' instead of 'it might rain'. Everyone knows how seriously to take it.
uk_angle: The NCSC and UK government assessments use this language. Using it in client reports makes your intel sound professional and makes it hard to misread.
enrichment_tip: After enriching a story, write one assessment sentence with a yardstick term, for example: 'It is likely (55-75%) that UK retailers will be targeted with this technique this quarter.'
try_today: Rewrite one headline from today's brief as a PHIA-style assessment sentence.
quiz_q: Which yardstick term covers roughly 55-75%?
quiz_a: Likely (or probable).

title: The intelligence cycle
explain: Intel work runs in a loop: Direction (what do we need to know?), Collection (gather data), Processing (clean and structure it), Analysis (make sense of it), Dissemination (share it), Feedback (was it useful?). Then round again.
analogy: Like cooking for a client: ask what they want to eat, buy ingredients, prep them, cook, serve, and ask how it tasted.
uk_angle: Most weak UK client intel programmes skip Direction and Feedback. They collect everything and ask nothing, so the output is noise.
enrichment_tip: Enrichment lives in Processing and Analysis. If you do not know the client's questions (Direction), you do not know which enrichment matters.
try_today: Write down one question a client of yours would want answered every morning. That is a requirement.
quiz_q: Which two stages of the cycle are most often skipped?
quiz_a: Direction (setting requirements) and Feedback.

title: Priority Intelligence Requirements (PIRs)
explain: PIRs are the handful of questions a client most needs answered, written down and agreed. Example: 'Is any ransomware group targeting UK law firms using our VPN vendor?' Every feed and enrichment step should serve at least one PIR.
analogy: A shopping list. Without one you come home with 40 things and forget the milk.
uk_angle: Tie PIRs to UK specifics: the client's sector, their regulator (FCA, ICO, Ofcom, Ofgem), their key suppliers, and their main technology.
enrichment_tip: Store PIRs per client as keywords (sector, vendors, brands). Then auto-tag every incoming story against them. This dashboard's sector tags are a first step.
try_today: Write three PIRs for one real or imagined UK client.
quiz_q: Why do PIRs make enrichment faster?
quiz_a: They tell you which context matters, so you only enrich what answers the client's questions.

title: Companies House as an enrichment source
explain: Companies House is the UK register of companies. Its free API returns a company's registered address, status, SIC codes (what industry it is in), officers (directors), filing history and parent companies.
analogy: A UK company's birth certificate, CV and family tree in one place.
uk_angle: When a UK victim appears on a ransomware leak site, Companies House tells you its sector, size and group structure. That lets you warn clients in the same sector or supply chain.
enrichment_tip: Map SIC codes to your sectors. For example 86xxx = human health, 64xxx = financial services, 69xxx = legal and accounting. Tag victims and clients the same way so matches are automatic.
try_today: Search a UK company from today's ransomware list at find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk and note its SIC code.
quiz_q: What does a SIC code tell you about a company?
quiz_a: Its industry or type of business activity.

title: IPs, ASNs and RIPE
explain: Every public IP belongs to a network called an Autonomous System, identified by an ASN (for example AS2856 is BT). RIPE NCC is the registry for Europe, including the UK. RIPEstat (stat.ripe.net) shows who owns an IP, its ASN, country and routing history for free.
analogy: The IP is a house number. The ASN is the estate or landlord who owns the whole street.
uk_angle: Knowing whether a malicious IP sits in a UK ASN changes the response. UK hosting means UK law enforcement and UK providers can act, and it may mean a compromised UK business rather than attacker-owned infrastructure.
enrichment_tip: Always add ASN name and country to an IP. Flag known residential ISPs (BT, Sky, Virgin Media) because these IPs are often compromised home devices or proxies, not attacker servers.
try_today: Look up one C2 IP from today's Feodo list on stat.ripe.net. Who owns it?
quiz_q: Which regional registry covers UK IP addresses?
quiz_a: RIPE NCC.

title: .uk domains, Nominet and WHOIS
explain: Nominet runs the .uk domain registry. WHOIS shows registration data such as registrar, creation date and name servers. Since GDPR most personal details are hidden, but creation date, registrar and name servers are still very useful.
analogy: WHOIS is the land registry for domains: you may not see the owner's name, but you see when the plot was bought and who sold it.
uk_angle: A lookalike .co.uk domain registered yesterday that imitates a client's brand is a strong phishing signal. New domain + brand name = high priority.
enrichment_tip: Add 'domain age in days' to every domain indicator. Domains under 30 days old deserve extra suspicion.
try_today: Run a WHOIS lookup on any .co.uk domain and find its creation date and registrar.
quiz_q: Why is domain age a useful enrichment field?
quiz_a: Newly registered domains are much more likely to be used for phishing or malware.

title: Passive DNS and certificate transparency
explain: Passive DNS is a history of which domains pointed to which IPs over time. Certificate transparency (crt.sh) logs every public TLS certificate issued. Together they let you pivot: from one bad domain to the IP, to other domains on that IP, to certificates with similar names.
analogy: Like checking who else has lived at a suspect's address over the years, and who else ordered the same custom number plate.
uk_angle: Search crt.sh for your clients' brand names (for example %clientname%) to find lookalike sites issued certificates, often before a phishing campaign starts.
enrichment_tip: A pivot is only useful with a limit. Record why each pivot is linked (same IP, same certificate, same registrar) and stop after two or three hops.
try_today: Search crt.sh for a UK brand name and see which subdomains and lookalikes appear.
quiz_q: What is 'pivoting' in threat intel?
quiz_a: Using one known indicator to discover related indicators, for example from a domain to its IP to other domains on that IP.

title: IOC vs IOA vs TTP
explain: An IOC (indicator of compromise) is evidence something bad happened: a hash, IP or domain. An IOA (indicator of attack) is behaviour showing an attack in progress, like PowerShell downloading a file and disabling antivirus. TTPs are the attacker's habits described in general terms.
analogy: IOC = fingerprints left at the scene. IOA = someone seen trying door handles right now. TTP = 'this gang always comes in through the back garden'.
uk_angle: Most free feeds give IOCs. Clients with a SIEM or EDR get more value if you translate IOCs into IOAs and detection ideas.
enrichment_tip: For every IOC batch, add one line: 'what behaviour would we see if this hit us?' That turns IOCs into IOAs.
try_today: Take one malware family from today's ThreatFox list and search for its common behaviour.
quiz_q: Is 'a new admin account created at 3am followed by backup deletion' an IOC or an IOA?
quiz_a: An IOA. It is suspicious behaviour, not a static artefact.

title: MITRE ATT&CK in five minutes
explain: ATT&CK is a free catalogue of attacker behaviour. Tactics are the attacker's goal (why), for example Initial Access. Techniques are how they achieve it, for example T1566 Phishing. Each technique has an ID, examples and detection advice.
analogy: A recipe book for attacks: tactics are chapters (starters, mains), techniques are individual recipes.
uk_angle: NCSC and Five Eyes joint advisories list ATT&CK IDs. Mapping them to a client's detections shows gaps in language their technical team understands.
enrichment_tip: When a story has no ATT&CK IDs, add them yourself: phishing email = T1566, valid stolen accounts = T1078, ransomware encryption = T1486.
try_today: Look up T1486 on attack.mitre.org and read the detection section.
quiz_q: What is the difference between a tactic and a technique?
quiz_a: A tactic is the goal (why). A technique is the method used to reach it (how).

title: The Diamond Model
explain: The Diamond Model describes every intrusion with four corners: Adversary (who), Capability (their tools), Infrastructure (servers, domains) and Victim (who was hit). If you know one corner, you can pivot to the others.
analogy: A crime scene board: suspect, weapon, getaway car, victim, with string between them.
uk_angle: For a UK ransomware victim: Victim from the leak site, Adversary = the gang, Capability = their ransomware, Infrastructure = their C2 and leak site. Each corner is an enrichment job.
enrichment_tip: Organise enrichment notes under the four corners. It shows at a glance which corner you know least about.
try_today: Fill in a diamond for one ransomware entry in today's brief. Which corners are empty?
quiz_q: Name the four corners of the Diamond Model.
quiz_a: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim.

title: The Cyber Kill Chain
explain: Lockheed Martin's Kill Chain splits an attack into seven stages: Reconnaissance, Weaponisation, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives. Stopping any stage breaks the chain.
analogy: Planning a burglary: case the house, get tools, approach, break the lock, move in, keep contact with the getaway driver, steal.
uk_angle: Great for explaining to UK client boards why a phishing email (Delivery) matters even if nobody clicked: it is a stage you already stopped.
enrichment_tip: Tag each IOC with its kill chain stage. A C2 IP is stage 6, so a hit on it means the attacker is already inside.
try_today: Place today's top story onto the kill chain. Which stage does it describe?
quiz_q: Which stage is a C2 (command and control) server?
quiz_a: Stage 6, Command and Control.

title: STIX, TAXII and MISP
explain: STIX is a standard format (JSON) for describing threat intel: indicators, malware, threat actors and the links between them. TAXII is a standard way to send STIX over the internet. MISP is popular free software for storing, enriching and sharing intel, and it speaks both.
analogy: STIX is the language, TAXII is the postal service, MISP is the filing cabinet and post room together.
uk_angle: Many UK sector sharing groups and MSSPs use MISP. Being able to export your enriched data as STIX makes it easy for clients' tools to consume.
enrichment_tip: Store enrichment as MISP attributes or tags (for example tlp:amber, admiralty-scale, sector) rather than free text, so machines can filter on them.
try_today: Open this dashboard's docs/data JSON file and spot which fields would become STIX indicators.
quiz_q: Which one is the format and which is the transport: STIX or TAXII?
quiz_a: STIX is the format. TAXII is the transport.

title: Indicators go stale: ageing and decay
explain: IOCs lose value over time. An IP used for C2 today may be a clean cloud server next month. Hashes stay accurate forever but the attacker stops using them. Good intel records first-seen and last-seen dates and expires old indicators.
analogy: Like milk: great today, questionable next week, harmful next month if you keep blocking with it.
uk_angle: Blocking a stale IP that now belongs to a UK cloud or CDN provider can break a client's business apps and destroy trust in your feed.
enrichment_tip: Add first_seen, last_seen and an expiry date to every IOC. A sensible default: IPs 30 days, domains 90 days, hashes much longer.
try_today: Check the last_online date on one Feodo C2 entry in today's brief. Would you still block it?
quiz_q: Why should IP indicators expire faster than hashes?
quiz_a: IPs get reassigned to new, often innocent, owners, while a hash always identifies the same file.

title: False positives and allowlists
explain: A false positive is a harmless thing flagged as malicious. Feeds sometimes include shared infrastructure like Google DNS (8.8.8.8), Microsoft or Cloudflare IPs. Blocking these can take a client offline. Allowlists (MISP calls them warninglists) catch them before sharing.
analogy: A smoke alarm that goes off every time you make toast. People soon take the battery out.
uk_angle: Add UK-specific allowlists: gov.uk, nhs.uk, major UK banks, and the client's own IP ranges and suppliers.
enrichment_tip: Before sharing any IOC, check it against an allowlist of popular domains (for example the Tranco top list) and cloud provider ranges.
try_today: List five domains that should never be blocked for a UK client.
quiz_q: What is a MISP warninglist for?
quiz_a: Flagging indicators that are probably false positives, such as well-known legitimate services.

title: Matching threats to client assets
explain: The most valuable enrichment is 'does this client have the thing?'. That needs an asset inventory: which vendors, products and versions each client runs, and which are internet facing. Vulnerabilities use CPE names (for example cpe:2.3:a:fortinet:fortios) to identify products.
analogy: A recall notice for a car is only useful if you know which car you drive.
uk_angle: Shodan and Censys searches with country:GB and a client's IP ranges show what they expose. Pair that with KEV each morning for a very high-value brief.
enrichment_tip: Keep a simple per-client file: vendor, product, internet facing (yes/no). Match each morning's CVEs against it. That is personalised intel.
try_today: Write down the five most important internet-facing products for one client (VPN, firewall, email, remote access, website CMS).
quiz_q: What does a CPE name identify?
quiz_a: A specific vendor and product (and optionally version) so vulnerabilities can be matched to it.

title: Cyber Essentials
explain: Cyber Essentials is the UK government-backed baseline certification. Five controls: firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection, and security update management. Cyber Essentials Plus adds a hands-on technical audit.
analogy: An MOT for a company's basic cyber hygiene.
uk_angle: Many UK public sector contracts require it. Framing intel around the five controls ('this CVE falls under security update management, 14-day rule') lands well with UK SMEs.
enrichment_tip: Tag each story with the Cyber Essentials control it relates to. Clients immediately see which part of their certification is under pressure.
try_today: Map today's top three stories to one of the five Cyber Essentials controls.
quiz_q: Name the five Cyber Essentials controls.
quiz_a: Firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection, security update management.

title: UK GDPR, the ICO and the 72-hour rule
explain: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 govern personal data in the UK. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) is the regulator. A personal data breach that poses a risk to people must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of it.
analogy: Like reporting a car accident to your insurer: there is a deadline, and missing it makes things worse.
uk_angle: When a UK breach hits the news, the regulatory angle (ICO report, possible fine) is often what gets a client's leadership to pay attention.
enrichment_tip: For breach stories, add a 'regulatory' field: ICO, FCA (finance), Ofcom (telecoms), NIS regulator (critical services). That shows clients who they might answer to.
try_today: Look at the ICO news feed in today's brief. Is there an enforcement action? What went wrong?
quiz_q: How long does a UK organisation have to report a qualifying personal data breach to the ICO?
quiz_a: 72 hours from becoming aware of it.

title: Where UK victims report things
explain: Suspicious emails: forward to report@phishing.gov.uk. Scam texts: forward to 7726. Fraud and cybercrime in England, Wales and Northern Ireland: the national fraud and cyber crime reporting service (Action Fraud, which is being replaced by a new Report Fraud service, so check which is live). Scotland: Police Scotland on 101. Significant incidents: the NCSC incident reporting service.
analogy: Knowing whether to call 999, 111 or your GP.
uk_angle: Clients value an analyst who tells them exactly where to report. Put the right channel in every relevant brief item.
enrichment_tip: Add a 'report to' field to phishing and fraud items with the correct UK channel for the client's nation.
try_today: Save these channels in your notes so you can paste them into client updates.
quiz_q: Where do UK users forward suspicious emails?
quiz_a: report@phishing.gov.uk.

title: Infostealers and stolen sessions
explain: Infostealers (for example Lumma, RedLine, Vidar) are malware that grab saved passwords, browser cookies and session tokens. Stolen sessions let attackers skip MFA. Logs get sold on criminal markets and often lead to ransomware or data theft weeks later.
analogy: Stealing someone's house key is bad. Stealing the key and the alarm code together is how people get in without a sound.
uk_angle: Many major breaches start with a stolen login. Checking whether client domains appear in stealer logs is high-value enrichment.
enrichment_tip: Watch for client email domains and SaaS login URLs in breach and stealer-log services, and treat a hit as an incident: reset passwords and revoke sessions.
try_today: Find one infostealer family in today's ThreatFox stats and read what it steals.
quiz_q: Why can a stolen session cookie bypass MFA?
quiz_a: It proves a login that already passed MFA, so the attacker does not have to log in again.

title: Help desk social engineering
explain: Groups like Scattered Spider phone IT help desks pretending to be staff and ask for password or MFA resets. No malware needed: they talk their way in, then add their own devices and move to ransomware or data theft.
analogy: Ringing the hotel reception, claiming you lost your room key, and being handed a new one.
uk_angle: Major UK retail attacks in 2025 were linked to this style of social engineering. It is a top concern for UK retail, finance and anyone with an outsourced help desk.
enrichment_tip: For identity attack stories, enrich with the targeted help desk provider or outsourcer. Clients sharing that supplier face higher risk.
try_today: Write three questions a help desk should ask before resetting MFA.
quiz_q: What does the attacker usually ask the help desk for?
quiz_a: A password reset or to register a new MFA device.

title: Typosquatting and brand monitoring
explain: Typosquatting means registering lookalike domains: cl1ent.co.uk, client-login.com, client.co instead of client.co.uk. Tools like dnstwist generate the possible variants and check which ones are registered.
analogy: A fake shop on the high street with a logo almost identical to the real one.
uk_angle: UK clients are often impersonated across .uk, .co.uk, .com and .org.uk. Monitoring all of these is cheap and catches phishing early.
enrichment_tip: For each lookalike: add creation date, whether it has MX records (can send or receive email), whether it has a live website, and certificate data from crt.sh.
try_today: Run dnstwist (pip install dnstwist) against a UK brand domain and count the registered lookalikes.
quiz_q: Why does an MX record on a lookalike domain matter?
quiz_a: It means the domain can handle email, so it can be used for phishing or invoice fraud.

title: Writing for clients: BLUF
explain: BLUF means Bottom Line Up Front. Start with the conclusion and the action, then give the detail. Busy readers stop after the first two lines, so those lines must carry the message.
analogy: A news headline and first paragraph tell you the whole story. The rest is for people who want more.
uk_angle: UK client boards and service desks both want: what happened, does it affect us, what do we do, by when.
enrichment_tip: Your enrichment should end in a BLUF line: 'Action: patch FortiOS on the two internet-facing firewalls today. KEV-listed, EPSS 94%.'
try_today: Write a two-line BLUF for today's number one story.
quiz_q: What does BLUF stand for?
quiz_a: Bottom Line Up Front.

title: Strategic, operational, tactical, technical
explain: Strategic intel is for leaders: trends and risk ('ransomware against UK retail is rising'). Operational is about specific campaigns and actors. Tactical covers TTPs for defenders. Technical is the raw IOCs for tools.
analogy: Planning a trip: the country's safety (strategic), a planned strike on travel day (operational), which neighbourhoods to avoid (tactical), the exact address of a pickpocket gang (technical).
uk_angle: A UK SME board needs strategic plus one action. Their MSP needs tactical and technical. Same enrichment, different packaging.
enrichment_tip: Tag each output with its level and audience so the right people get the right version.
try_today: Rewrite one story from today's brief at the strategic level for a board.
quiz_q: Which level of intel is a list of malicious IPs?
quiz_a: Technical.

title: Evaluating feeds
explain: Not every feed is worth ingesting. Judge feeds on: relevance (does it cover threats to your clients?), timeliness, accuracy (false positive rate), completeness (context included?), and uniqueness (does it overlap with what you already have?).
analogy: Choosing newspapers: some are fast but wrong, some are slow but careful, some just copy each other.
uk_angle: Check how much of a feed is UK-relevant. A feed with lots of US-only activity may be noise for UK clients.
enrichment_tip: Use the Source health table at the bottom of this dashboard and track which feeds produce stories you actually forward to clients.
try_today: Look at today's Source health table. Which feed gave the most UK-relevant items?
quiz_q: Name three criteria for evaluating a threat feed.
quiz_a: Any three of: relevance, timeliness, accuracy, completeness, uniqueness.

title: Building a UK relevance score
explain: A relevance score combines simple signals into one number so you know what to read first. This dashboard adds points for UK keywords, UK sources, KEV status, EPSS, severity, threat type, freshness and corroboration. Every point is explained in the 'why' line.
analogy: A credit score for news stories: many small signals turned into one number you can sort by.
uk_angle: Tune the weights to your clients: a legal-sector client should boost 'law firm' and 'solicitor'; a council client should boost 'council' and 'public sector'.
enrichment_tip: Keep scoring explainable. If a client asks 'why is this top?', you should be able to point to each factor.
try_today: Open ti/enrich.py and find UK_TERMS. Add one keyword that matters to your clients.
quiz_q: Why should a relevance score be explainable?
quiz_a: So analysts and clients can trust it, challenge it and tune it.

title: Critical national infrastructure and NIS
explain: CNI covers services the UK depends on: energy, water, transport, health, telecoms, finance, government and more. The NIS Regulations 2018 set security duties for operators of essential services and some digital providers, and many are assessed against the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF). The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill is set to widen these rules, so check its current status.
analogy: The load-bearing walls of the country. Everything else leans on them.
uk_angle: If a client is a CNI operator or supplies one, nation-state and OT (operational technology) stories get a much higher priority.
